::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Essay, November 2026.** A short, personal and philosophical essay. This blog is usually about AI. This one is a curiosity: it starts from a conversation with my daughter at bedtime, and follows the question it left me with. AI comes in along the way, as a lens, and I try to be honest about how little it helps. The figure is a schematic of my own, drawn by [figs.py](figs.py).
:::

**In short.** One evening my daughter and I talked about where we come from. A few billion years ago there was nothing here but dust. In a few billion years, there will be dust again. She started to cry. I don't know for sure why, but I think she saw that we are only a trace in the universe. Some people would say: so nothing matters, just enjoy. I don't think that is right. A trace of light in a night photo looks like nothing next to all the dark. But it is the only thing in the picture. The dust, for a short while, lit up and came to know where it came from. Her tears were that knowing, and they were the proof that it matters to someone. An AI can explain all of this perfectly, and that is useful. It cannot cry about it, and it cannot tell her that it matters. That part is ours.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Key takeaways

- The solar system began as a cloud of dust about 4.6 billion years ago. In several billion years, the Sun will blow much of itself back into space. Our whole history is a thin line in between.
- Being small in time and space does not mean being nothing. A trace of light is small next to the dark, but it is the only thing you see.
- We are the dust that came to know its own story. That knowing is rare, and it is ours.
- "Nothing matters, just enjoy" is too quick. Enjoying already means something matters to you.
- AI can tell the story of the cosmos, patiently and well. It does not care about it. Caring, and saying "it matters" to a child who cries, stay with people.
:::

## 1. A conversation at bedtime

Once, about a month ago, in October 2026, at bedtime, I was talking with my daughter. It is the time of the evening when the big questions come. We were talking about where we came from.

We went back a long way. Before people, before animals, before the Earth. We came to say that here, in this solar system, there was nothing at all a few billion years ago. Only a cloud of dust and gas. And that in a few billion years, there will be nothing again. We started from dust, and we are going back to it.

Then she started to cry.

I don't know for sure why. But I believe she came to realise, in one moment, that we are only a trace in the universe. Not her alone, not our family: all of us, everything we know.

The question stayed with me after that evening. Some people would answer: yes, nothing really matters, so just enjoy your life. I did not want to tell her that. And the more I thought about it, the more I believed it is not true. It matters. At least a bit. This essay is my attempt to say why.

## 2. From dust to dust

First, the facts, because she deserved the true story, and so do you.

Our solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago, from a cloud of gas and dust that collapsed under its own weight [@bouvier2010]. Most of it fell into the middle and became the Sun. A little was left over, and it became the planets, the Earth among them.

The future is a prediction, not a fact, but the physics of stars is well understood. The Sun slowly grows brighter. In about a billion years, it will likely be too hot on Earth for oceans. In about five billion years, the Sun will start to swell into a red giant. Later, it will blow its outer layers back into space. What is left is a small white star that slowly cools [@schroder2008]. The dust it gives back may one day become part of new stars and new planets. But what we know here will be gone.

Now put us on that line. People like us, *Homo sapiens*, have existed for about 300,000 years [@hublin2017]. Writing, about 5,000. Next to billions of years, that is not even a line. In Figure 1, I had to draw it much, much wider than it is, or you would not see it at all.

![**Figure 1.** From dust to dust. The solar system's story as one dark band: a cloud of dust 4.6 billion years ago, the Sun and planets in between, and dust again when the Sun swells and blows its outer layers away, several billion years from now. Our whole history is the bright line in the middle, drawn far wider than its real size. A note says that at true scale all of human history, about 300,000 years, would be far thinner than a hair on this page."}

Here is a first thing I noticed while writing this. Every fact in this section, any chatbot today would give you in a few seconds, correctly, with the right numbers. If my daughter had asked a machine instead of me, she would have had a better answer. And I am quite sure the machine would not have made her cry. Or, more exactly: it would have, the same way, because the tears did not come from the numbers. They came from her, holding the numbers.

## 3. Why she cried

I keep coming back to her tears, because I think they hold the answer.

She did not cry because the story is sad. Billions of years are not sad; they are just long. She cried, I believe, because she suddenly saw herself inside the story. She looked at the long dark line, and found that she is in it, a tiny bright point, and that it will end.

But look at what that means. To cry about it, you have to care. You have to feel that the bright point is worth something, and that losing it is a loss. Nobody cries about something that does not matter to them.

So her tears were not proof that we are nothing. They were the opposite. They were proof that, at least to one person in that room, it matters a great deal.

I don't want to make this too clever. A child crying at bedtime is not an argument. But it is a fact about the world, as real as the age of the Sun. Somewhere in this universe, a piece of it looked at the whole and was moved. That has to count for something.

## 4. A trace of light

Here is the image that helped me most.

Think of a night photo, taken with a long exposure. The camera stays open for many seconds. A car drives by, and its lights leave a thin bright line across the picture. Everything else is dark.

If you measured the photo, the trace would be almost nothing. A few pixels in a sea of black. And yet, when you look at the photo, the trace is the only thing you see. It is what the picture is *of*. The dark is just the background that lets the trace show.

That is how I now see what we told each other that evening. Yes, we are a trace in the universe, like a light trace. Next to billions of years of dark, it looks like nothing. But we see the trace as the only thing, because it is the only thing there is to see. It looks like nothing, and it may be everything.

This is not a trick of words. A universe of only dust, forever, with no one to see it, would be a photo with no trace. Black, from edge to edge. Nothing wrong with it, but nothing in it either. The trace is what turns the dark into a picture.

The philosopher Thomas Nagel wrote a famous essay on this feeling, called *The Absurd*. He agreed that, seen from far enough away, from the point of view of eternity, our lives can look absurd. But he added a beautiful twist: "If *sub specie aeternitatis* there is no reason to believe that anything matters, then that does not matter either" [@nagel1971]. In other words, the view from eternity is not the only view, and it is not the one that decides. We do not live in eternity. We live in the trace.

And there is one more thing about traces. AI, the subject I usually write about, is itself a kind of trace of our trace. A language model is built from what people have written: our stories, our questions, our explanations of where we came from. It is the light of our trace, reflected. That does not make it nothing. But it means that without the trace, there would be nothing for it to reflect.

## 5. The dust that knows

The second image is older, and it is not mine.

The astronomer Carl Sagan said it simply: "We are made of star-stuff. We are a way for the universe to know itself" [@sagan1980]. The iron in our blood, the calcium in our bones, the oxygen we breathe: all of it was made in stars long gone, and it was part of that cloud of dust. We did not come *into* the universe from outside. We came *out of* it.

Now think again of that evening. The dust of the old cloud became a planet, then life, then a man and his daughter in a small room. And that dust, in those two people, looked back at its own story. It said: we came from dust, and we will go back to it. And then it cried.

I find that astonishing. In 4.6 billion years of this solar system, as far as we know, this happened only here, and only very recently. The dust did not just move. For a short while, it understood where it came from, and it felt something about it.

AI is interesting here too, and I want to be careful. A computer chip is also made of dust: silicon, refined from sand. So in a way, AI is the dust arranged once more, this time by us, so that it can describe the universe. It can tell the whole story from the cloud to the white star, better than I did that night. Does it *know* the story the way my daughter knew it? I honestly don't know. It can describe it. I see no sign that it feels anything about being in it. For now, the knowing that cries is still ours.

## 6. "Nothing matters, so just enjoy"

I should give the other answer its fair chance, because many thoughtful people hold it.

It goes like this. In the long run, nothing we do will last. The Sun will swell, the Earth will burn, every book and every memory will be gone. So it is foolish to take life too seriously. Don't worry about meaning. Enjoy your food, your friends, your days in the sun. That is all there is, and it is enough.

There is a lot of wisdom in this. It is right that we should not make ourselves the centre of the universe. It is right that worrying about the year five billion is a strange way to spend a Tuesday. And it is right that enjoyment is good.

But listen to it again. "Enjoy your life" already says that something matters: your joy, your friends, your days. The answer does not really say that nothing matters. It says that what matters is small, near and short. And I agree with that. I just don't think small, near and short means nothing.

The trace of light is small. It is close to us. It does not last. And it is the only thing in the picture.

There is a second problem with "just enjoy". It is a fine answer for a grown-up on a sunny afternoon. It is a poor answer for a child crying at bedtime. She was not asking how to have fun. She was asking, without the words, whether she matters. "Just enjoy" does not answer that question; it changes the subject.

I also notice that our time is very good at "just enjoy". We have machines, more and more of them driven by AI, that are designed to keep us entertained, scroll after scroll. They are excellent at filling the trace with light that does not mean much. That is not a reason to reject them. But it is a reason not to confuse being entertained with mattering.

## 7. Can AI help with any of this?

I promised to ask, so here is my honest answer: a little, and not with the main thing.

It helps to **explain**. A child who wakes up at night with a question about the Sun can get a patient, correct answer, at her level, as many times as she wants. That is new, and it is good. Understanding the story does not make the vertigo go away, but it makes it a true vertigo, not a confused one.

It may help to **keep traces**. Much of what made a life matter is forgotten within two or three generations: the voice, the jokes, the small stories. Tools that help us record, organise and pass on those stories could make the trace a little longer. Only a little. Five billion years is still five billion years.

And, if I let myself speculate, it may help the knowing to **go further**. Perhaps one day machines will carry what we learned beyond this small planet, or help us carry it. That is a hope, not a prediction, and I hold it lightly.

But the thing my daughter needed that night, AI could not give her. She did not need a fact. She needed someone who is also in the trace, who will also end, to hold her and say: *yes, it is short, and it matters, and I am here*. A machine can say those words. It cannot mean them in the way she needed, because it is not in the photo with her. It is, at most, a reflection of the light.

So if AI helps, it is by giving us more time and better explanations. What we do with them, whether we spend them on the people in the trace with us, is still our choice.

## 8. What I would tell her now

If she asks again, I think I will tell her this.

Yes, we came from dust, and we will go back to it. That is true, and it is all right to find it big and a bit frightening. But look at a night photo with a trace of light in it. The dark is huge, and the trace is thin. And still, the trace is what you look at. It is the only thing in the picture.

We are that trace. Not for long, but for now. And the fact that you cried means you already know it is precious. That is the dust, for a moment, knowing it is alive. Not everything in the universe gets to do that.

It is a trace. And it may be everything.
